asbestos.types: Asbestos minerals are classified for regulation, not for purchase. Regulators distinguish chrysotile, the serpentine form behind most historical use, from the amphiboles crocidolite, amosite, tremolite, anthophyllite and actinolite. Historically, the long fibers suited to spinning were graded for textiles, while shorter grades went into cement sheet, floor tile, friction products and insulation. In the United States, the EPA's 2024 rule addressed the last known ongoing uses of chrysotile: diaphragms in chlor-alkali plants, sheet gaskets, oilfield brake blocks, aftermarket automotive brakes and linings, and other vehicle friction products. This entry describes these categories only for historical and regulatory context.
asbestos.fabrics: Historical asbestos textiles included woven cloth, tape, rope, yarn, lagging and felt, used in fire blankets, heat-resistant gloves and aprons, theater safety curtains, boiler and stove door rope seals, pipe and duct wrap, electrical insulation and laboratory equipment. Asbestos was often blended with a carrier fiber such as cotton to make it spinnable. Such items can survive in old buildings, ships, workshops, laboratories and collections, which is why museums and property owners treat unknown vintage heat-resistant textiles with caution.
asbestos.quality: This atlas gives no buying, selling or handling advice for asbestos. Asbestos is banned or restricted in many countries; the International Ban Asbestos Secretariat lists national bans in roughly 70 countries, with 2025 totals varying by source and by how partial bans are counted. Legacy items are the realistic concern: old fire blankets, gloves, rope gaskets, lagging and lab mats that are gray-white, stiff or felt-like may contain asbestos, but appearance cannot confirm it. If an item is suspected, do not buy, sell, use or disturb it; only an accredited laboratory sample taken by a qualified professional can establish its content.
pros: Historically it resisted heat and fire, which drove its use in protective and insulating products.
It could be spun and woven like a textile fiber.
It resisted many chemicals and was cheap, which explains its once-wide adoption.
These historical properties do not justify any current use.
cons: IARC classifies all forms of asbestos as carcinogenic to humans (Group 1).
Inhaled fibers cause asbestosis, lung cancer and mesothelioma, often decades after exposure.
Legacy material in buildings, vehicles and products still exposes workers and occupants when disturbed.
Removal and disposal are costly and must follow strict regulations.
asbestos.impact: Asbestos's footprint is measured in disease. Beyond the annual death toll estimates in the research profile, chrysotile is still mined and used in some countries while dozens of others have banned it. In the United States, the EPA published its Part 1 chrysotile rule under TSCA section 6 on 28 March 2024, effective 28 May 2024, banning the remaining known uses with phased compliance dates. Industry groups challenged it in the Fifth Circuit; in 2025 EPA sought time to reconsider parts of the rule, then withdrew that motion in July 2025, leaving the rule in place while litigation continued. Legacy asbestos in buildings and waste remains the main exposure route.
asbestos.care: Do not disturb. Suspected asbestos textiles or materials should not be cut, brushed, washed, vacuumed, repaired, moved, bagged or thrown out by an untrained person. Keep people away from damaged material and leave assessment, sampling, removal and disposal to licensed asbestos professionals working under the rules of the jurisdiction, such as EPA and OSHA requirements in the United States or national rules implementing EU directives. Museums and owners of historic collections should consult conservators and licensed assessors. This is general safety information, not legal or professional advice.
faq: Is asbestos banned in the United States?

The EPA's 2024 TSCA rule bans the remaining known uses of chrysotile asbestos, with phased deadlines, and was in effect as of the sources reviewed, though litigation continued. Older asbestos in buildings is not removed by the rule and is managed under separate abatement and workplace regulations.

No. Many countries, including all EU member states, have national bans, and the International Ban Asbestos Secretariat's list counted roughly 70 countries in 2025, with totals varying by source. Chrysotile is still mined and used elsewhere, so bans remain uneven.
How can I tell if an old fire blanket contains asbestos?

You cannot tell by look or feel. Only an accredited laboratory analyzing a sample taken by a qualified professional can confirm it. Leave the item undisturbed, keep people away if it is damaged, and contact a licensed asbestos assessor.
Is chrysotile safer than other asbestos?

Chrysotile is less biopersistent than amphiboles and less potent for mesothelioma, but IARC classifies all asbestos forms, chrysotile included, as carcinogenic to humans. Regulators treat it as a serious hazard, which is why the EPA's 2024 rule targeted it.
notable: The EPA's 2024 chrysotile rule was the first ban finalized under the agency's revised TSCA section 6 authority.
Among the last US uses of chrysotile were diaphragms in chlor-alkali plants that make chlorine and caustic soda.
In June 2025 EPA told the Fifth Circuit it planned to reconsider parts of its chrysotile rule, then withdrew that request the following month.
